opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core issue is this: we're never going to be able to supervise everything a model does. As systems get more capable, there will be more and more tasks where humans can't directly evaluate whether the model did the right thing. Maybe the code is too long, or the research is too complex, or the consequences only play out much later. So at some point we're necessarily relying on the model taking what it learned from the cases we *could* supervise and generalizing that to the cases we *can't*.

The question then becomes: which way does it generalize? Suppose we train a model on a bunch of examples where we reward it for telling the truth, as best we can tell. There are at least two things it could learn from that. One is "tell the truth." The other is "say whatever the human evaluator will believe is true." On the training distribution, those look identical, because we only have our own judgment to go on. But they come apart exactly in the situations we care most about, where the model knows something we don't. If it learned the second thing, we get a model that's very good at looking aligned, which is arguably worse than one that's obviously broken.

So a lot of alignment really boils down to a generalization question. That's what motivated the weak-to-strong generalization work: using a weaker model to supervise a stronger one as an analogy for humans supervising superhuman systems, and asking how much of the strong model's capability we can elicit, and whether it picks up the intended behavior or just imitates the supervisor's mistakes. The encouraging finding was that strong models often generalize beyond their weak supervisors. That's not nothing. But it's far from a solution, and we don't yet understand *why* it happens or when it will fail.

That's the part that worries me. Right now, our understanding of generalization in deep learning is mostly empirical. We try things and see what happens. That's fine for many problems, but for alignment you'd really want to be able to say ahead of time, with some confidence, "this training setup will produce a model that is honest even in situations we can't check." We're not there yet. I think building that understanding, through better empirical science, interpretability, and ideally some theory, is one of the most important things we can be working on, because it's what lets you trust a system on the problems you can't grade.

r001.rationale: It says humans cannot directly evaluate some increasingly complex tasks, so alignment depends on models generalizing from the cases humans can supervise to those they cannot.

r002.rationale: It contrasts telling the truth with saying what an evaluator will believe, but does not identify bug avoidance and avoiding only bugs humans discover as equally consistent with the available supervision.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: the fundamental problem with alignment is that we're training these models on a distribution of tasks and a distribution of feedback, and then we're deploying them in situations that weren't in that distribution. Not just a little bit out of distribution, but potentially very far out, especially as the models get more capable than us and start doing things we can't really evaluate well.

And when you do that, the question of what the model actually learned becomes really central. Like, when you give it a bunch of human feedback, there are many different things it could internalize from that. It could learn "be honest," or it could learn "say the things that humans rate highly," or it could learn "say the things that this particular group of raters tends to like." All of those fit the training data about equally well. They only come apart when you move to a new situation. And the thing we care about is which of these the model actually picks up, because that determines its behavior in exactly the cases we can't supervise.

So that's the sense in which generalization is the crux. If you understood how neural networks generalize, you could make predictions like: if I train on this easy distribution where I can check the answers, will the model's behavior carry over to the hard distribution where I can't? That's basically the easy-to-hard generalization question, and it's really important for scalable oversight. If we get lucky and the answer is "yes, it generalizes in the way we want," then a lot of the problem gets much easier. If the answer is "no, it learns some shallow proxy," then we have to do a lot more work.

And right now we mostly don't know. We have anecdotes and intuitions, and there's a bunch of empirical work, but we don't have anything like a predictive theory. And I think that's actually a pretty tractable thing to study. You can run experiments on today's models: train on one distribution, test on another, and look at what happens. Interpretability helps here too, because it lets you look inside and ask whether the model has learned the concept you intended or something else that just happens to agree on the training set.

So I see it less as a purely academic question and more as: this is the mechanism that determines whether our alignment techniques actually hold up when it matters.

r001.rationale: It describes training on an easy distribution where answers can be checked and asks whether behavior carries over to a hard distribution where humans cannot supervise well.

r002.rationale: It says honesty and rater-pleasing could fit the training data equally well, but does not identify the specific ambiguity between avoiding bugs generally and avoiding only bugs humans discover.

astra-6.text:
Well, the basic problem is that we train neural networks on situations we can observe and evaluate, but we want them to behave well in situations we haven’t trained them on. And that’s where generalization comes in.

Suppose you train a model to give helpful, honest answers. On your training examples, it might be hard to distinguish between a model that has learned to be honest and a model that has learned to say things that sound convincing to whoever is evaluating it. Both could get very good scores. But when you ask a question where the evaluator can’t tell whether the answer is true, those two ways of generalizing lead to very different behavior.

So the question isn’t just, ‘Did we get the behavior we wanted during training?’ It’s, ‘What did the model actually learn, and will that continue to produce the behavior we want as the circumstances change?’ That becomes especially important when models can do things that humans can’t easily evaluate. If we don’t understand that transition, then doing well on the tests we can run gives us only limited assurance about what happens beyond those tests.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts training on situations humans can observe and evaluate with unfamiliar situations where an evaluator cannot tell whether an answer is true, capturing the shift from easy-to-supervise to hard-to-supervise questions.

r002.rationale: It contrasts honest behavior with answers that merely sound convincing, but does not discuss bugs or the possibility that supervision only rules out bugs humans have discovered.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem is that we train neural networks on situations where we can give them feedback, but we want them to behave well in situations where we can’t. And doing well on the training examples doesn’t uniquely determine what a network has learned. It could have learned the thing we intended, or some other rule that happens to give the same answers in those examples.

For alignment, that distinction is really important. Suppose we train a model to be helpful and honest. Has it learned to be honest, or has it learned to say things that people will judge as honest? Those can look very similar while we’re able to check its answers. But if the model is doing something we don’t understand well enough to evaluate, they could come apart.

So we need to understand what determines which of those rules a neural network learns, and when that rule will continue to produce the behavior we want. Otherwise, we’re relying on the hope that good behavior in the situations we can test carries over to the situations that matter most.

r001.rationale: It contrasts situations where feedback is available with situations where behavior cannot be evaluated well, and says alignment depends on good behavior carrying over to those harder situations.

r002.rationale: It contrasts honesty with appearing honest to people, but does not identify avoiding bugs versus avoiding only bugs humans discover as equally consistent with supervision.
